Issue: Attempts to collect debt not owed
Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting this complaint to dispute a derogatory account being reported by Barclays Bank Delaware on my consumer credit report. This account is being reported as a charge-off with a past-due balance, even though I do not own this account and never authorized it. The account is the direct result of identity theft. 

I did not apply for, open, authorize, sign for, or use any credit account with Barclays Bank Delaware. I have never entered into any contractual relationship with this company, nor have I received goods, services, or credit from Barclays Bank Delaware. Any account Barclays claims is associated with me was opened fraudulently by an unknown third party without my knowledge or consent. 

I first became aware of this account when reviewing my credit report and seeing that Barclays Bank Delaware was reporting a charged-off credit card account with a balance that exceeded the original credit limit. The account was listed as delinquent and derogatory, which immediately raised concern because I have no history with this company and did not recognize the account. 

After discovering this account, I took prompt and responsible action to protect myself. I filed an identity theft report with the Federal Trade Commission ( FTC ) and began disputing the account as fraudulent. I notified the credit reporting agencies and Barclays Bank Delaware that this account does not belong to me and that it was the result of identity theft. 

Despite being notified that the account was fraudulent and that I had filed an FTC identity theft report, Barclays Bank Delaware has continued to report this account as a valid charge-off. The account remains on my credit report with a balance and past-due amount, which is inaccurate and misleading. 

As part of my dispute, I requested that Barclays Bank Delaware provide proof that I am the rightful account holder. Specifically, I requested documentation such as a signed credit application, a signed cardholder agreement, proof of identity verification used at account opening, billing statements showing my use of the account, or any evidence demonstrating that I knowingly agreed to or benefited from this debt. 

Barclays Bank Delaware has failed to provide any such documentation. Instead, it appears that the company is relying on internal records or automated systems to justify its reporting. The mere existence of an account number or internal data does not establish that I opened or authorized the account. Without a signed agreement or proof of authorization, Barclays Bank Delaware can not reasonably or lawfully attribute this account to me. 

Under federal law, once a consumer reports identity theft and submits an FTC identity theft report, companies are required to take reasonable steps to ensure that fraudulent information is not reported. The Fair Credit Reporting Act requires that inaccurate information not be furnished and that information resulting from identity theft be blocked or removed. Barclays Bank Delawares continued reporting of this account after being notified of identity theft is unreasonable and inconsistent with these obligations. 

The ongoing reporting of this fraudulent charge-off has caused harm. It falsely portrays me as having defaulted on a credit obligation that I never incurred. It negatively affects my creditworthiness and creates an inaccurate credit profile. This harm is significant because it is based entirely on fraudulent activity committed by someone else. 

In addition, the way Barclays Bank Delaware has handled this dispute raises concerns about the adequacy of its investigation process. A reasonable investigation must determine whether the consumer actually opened and authorized the account. Simply verifying that data matches internal records or that an account exists is not sufficient. A proper investigation requires confirmation of identity and authorization at account opening. 

I have acted in good faith throughout this process. I promptly disputed the account, filed an FTC identity theft report, and requested verification. Barclays Bank Delaware has not met its corresponding responsibility to ensure accuracy before continuing to report negative information. 

I am not disputing this account due to dissatisfaction with interest rates, fees, or payment terms. I am disputing it because the account is not mine. I did not open it, I did not authorize it, and I do not owe the alleged debt. 

I am requesting that Barclays Bank Delaware be required to take corrective action to resolve this issue. This includes stopping the reporting of this account, deleting it from my credit report, and acknowledging that the account resulted from identity theft. 

Identity theft victims should not be required to repeatedly dispute fraudulent accounts or suffer ongoing damage to their credit due to a companys failure to properly investigate. Continuing to report this account after notice of identity theft is unfair and harmful. 

I am seeking the CFPBs assistance to ensure that Barclays Bank Delaware complies with federal consumer protection laws, corrects the inaccurate reporting, and prevents further harm caused by this fraudulent charge-off account.

STATEMENT OF FACTS AND LEGAL VIOLATIONS Payment Made and Account Standing On or about XX/XX/XXXX, the Complainant, XXXX XXXX, paid the remaining balance owed on his secured credit account in the amount of {$260.00} to Defendant Self Financial , Inc. ( Self ). This account is a secured credit line, funded by the Complainants own money, and was established for the express purpose of building credit. 
Improper Rejection of Lawful Payment Method Despite the payment being valid and lawful, Self failed to properly recognize or process the Complainants primary bank account. As a direct result of Selfs failure, the Complainant was forced to use a secondary payment method. The Complainant informed Self that this was the only bank account available to him, as all attempts to open additional bank accounts had been denied. 
Notice of Federal Law Violations The Complainant explicitly informed Self that denying or mishandling lawful payments on a secured credit account, and threatening adverse action as a result, constituted violations of federal consumer protection laws, including but not limited to : Truth in Lending Act ( TILA ), 15 U.S.C. 1601 et seq., which requires accurate account administration and prohibits unfair or deceptive practices involving credit accounts ; Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( EFTA ), 15 U.S.C. 1693 et seq., which protects consumers from improper handling of electronic payments ; Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681 et seq., which prohibits furnishing inaccurate or misleading information and requires reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy ; Unfair, Deceptive, or Abusive Acts or Practices ( UDAAP ) under 12 U.S.C. 5531, enforced by the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ).

The Complainant further demanded that his secured payment be properly credited within XXXX hours, warning that failure to do so would constitute a willful violation of federal law. 
Improper Account Closure and False Attribution On or about XX/XX/XXXX, Self unilaterally closed the Complainants secured credit account, citing an alleged statement that the Complainant had requested closure during a prior telephone call on XXXX. This allegation is categorically false. 
At no time did the Complainant : Request account closure ; Provide written authorization to close the account ; Consent to termination of the secured credit line. 
Selfs own policies require verification and confirmation prior to closing a consumer credit account. No such verification occurred. 
Retaliation and Bad Faith The closure occurred immediately after the Complainant asserted his legal rights and objected to federal law violations. The timing and circumstances demonstrate retaliation, bad faith, and willful misconduct, particularly given that the account was secured by the Complainants own funds. 
Frustration expressed by the Complainant during the call was a direct result of Defendants unlawful conduct and does not constitute consent to account termination. 
LEGAL VIOLATIONS Federal Law Violations Truth in Lending Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1605, 1638 ) Improper administration and termination of a secured credit account without authorization or proper disclosure.

Electronic Fund Transfer Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1693f ) Failure to properly process and investigate electronic payments.

Fair Credit Reporting Act ( 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ) Furnishing or causing inaccurate account status information and failing to follow reasonable procedures.

CFPB UDAAP Provisions ( 12 U.S.C. 5531 & 5536 ) Retaliatory account closure, misrepresentation, and abusive conduct. 
State Law Violations ( Generally Applicable ) Breach of Contract Breach of the Covenant of Good Faith and Fair Dealing Conversion of Secured Funds Negligent and/or Intentional Misrepresentation Consumer Protection Act Violations ( state-specific ) SUPPORTING CASE LAW ( Illustrative ) Johnson v. MBNA America Bank, N.A. , 357 F.3d 426 ( 4th Cir. 2004 ) Creditors must conduct reasonable investigations and may not rely on false internal assertions.

Safeco Ins. Co. v. Burr, 551 U.S. 47 ( 2007 ) Willful violations include reckless disregard of statutory duties.

Spokeo , Inc. v. Robins, 578 U.S. 330 ( 2016 ) Inaccurate credit handling constitutes concrete consumer harm.

In re Sanchez, 941 F.3d 625 ( 2d Cir. 2019 ) Retaliatory conduct following assertion of statutory rights is actionable. 
SUMMARY Defendant Self Financial , Inc. unlawfully mishandled a secured payment, retaliated against the Complainant for asserting federally protected rights, falsely attributed consent to close the account, and terminated a secured credit line without authorization, in violation of federal and state law.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am filing a complaint regarding CRIs credit reporting practices related to my federal student loans. 

I have a long history of responsible, on-time payment across all of my student loans, which were typically managed and paid as a group. Automatic payments had been enabled and used successfully over an extended period. 

Without my intent or awareness, automatic payments were turned off. As a result, I fell behind unintentionally. Once the issue was discovered, I took steps to bring the account back into good standing. 

Because my loans are reported as multiple separate tradelines, this single lapse resulted in delinquency being reported simultaneously on ten separate accounts. This created a severe and disproportionate negative impact on my credit profile that does not accurately reflect my overall payment behavior or creditworthiness.

While CRI states that reporting at 90 days past due is required, my concern is not simply that a delinquency was reported, but that : - Autopay termination was not clearly disclosed or reasonably noticeable - A single oversight resulted in multiple simultaneous derogatory tradelines - No individualized review was conducted to assess proportionality or borrower intent - Frontline customer service stated that goodwill review is categorically unavailable, without addressing the underlying fairness or accuracy concerns I am requesting that CRI conduct a formal compliance review of : - Whether XXXX termination notice met disclosure requirements - Whether the credit reporting accurately and fairly reflects the circumstances - Whether any correction, adjustment, or alternative reporting is appropriate given the unique impact of this event I am not disputing that payments were missed. I am disputing whether the reporting as furnished is fair, proportional, and compliant given the circumstances. 

I am seeking resolution through review and correction where appropriate. 

Thank you for your attention to this matter.

Account paid from collateral, removal file from credit, no payments were made, remove as soon as possible Subject : Federal Laws Governing Removal of Credit File Information Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681, consumer reporting agencies may include only information that is accurate, verifiable, and legally permissible. Pursuant to 15 U.S.C. 1681e ( b ), agencies and furnishers must follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy. Information that is inaccurate or can not be verified may not remain in a consumer file.

Under 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ), when any item of information is disputed, a consumer reporting agency must conduct a reasonable reinvestigation. Any information found to be inaccurate, incomplete, or unverifiable must be deleted from the consumers credit file.

Under 15 U.S.C. 1681c, consumer reporting agencies are prohibited from retaining obsolete information beyond statutory time limits, including outdated adverse items. Information that exceeds allowable reporting periods must be removed from the file. 

Under 15 U.S.C. 1681b, a consumer reporting agency may only maintain or disclose information for a lawful permissible purpose. Information lacking a permissible purpose or lawful attribution may not be retained in a consumer file.

Willful or negligent noncompliance with the FCRA is subject to civil liability under 15 U.S.C. 1681n and 1681o.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am submitting this response as part of a new CFPB case, as my prior case # XXXX was closed without resolving the underlying dispute or requiring Kikoff Lending , LLC to provide legally sufficient proof of account ownership. The closure of that prior case does not cure the continued reporting and defense of an account that I do not own and did not authorize. Accordingly, this submission represents a renewed and active dispute that requires further CFPB review. 

I respectfully but firmly disagree with XXXX XXXX response and conclusions. I do not own this account, I did not open it, I did not authorize it, and I did not knowingly benefit from it. This account is the result of identity theft, which is why I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report and identity theft affidavit in good faith and in compliance with federal law. My dispute is not based on dissatisfaction with account terms, payment schedules, or customer service ; it is based solely on fraud and identity theft. 

1. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX states that its internal investigation found insufficient evidence to support removal of the account and that its findings remain unchanged. However, an internal investigation that relies primarily on XXXX own systems, records, and processes does not meet the standard of a reasonable investigation under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ) when identity theft has been asserted. 

A reasonable investigation requires more than confirming that an account exists in a database or that certain system checks were completed. It requires determining whether the account was lawfully opened and authorized by the consumer. Internal consistency is not proof of authorization. In identity theft cases, internal records are often the very records created as a result of the fraud. 

2. Multifactor Authentication Does Not Prove Account Ownership Kikoff places significant weight on the assertion that multifactor authentication ( XXXX ) was used during account creation and verification. XXXX, however, does not establish that I personally opened or authorized the account. 

Identity theft frequently involves : Compromised email accounts XXXX swapping or phone number takeovers Intercepted verification codes Unauthorized access to personal devices Successful XXXX only demonstrates that someone had access to a communication channel at a given moment. It does not prove that the lawful consumer knowingly entered into a binding credit agreement. Treating XXXX as conclusive proof of ownership is inconsistent with the realities of modern identity theft and improperly shifts the burden of proof onto the victim. 

3. Generic Electronic Agreement Is Not Proof of Consent Kikoff references an electronically completed credit agreement and attaches a standard Credit Account Agreement. However, the document provided is a boilerplate agreement template that applies to all accounts. It does not contain : My signature ( wet or authenticated electronic ) A timestamped signature record IP address or device identifiers tied to me Geolocation data Third-party identity verification results A generic agreement without proof of execution does not establish that I agreed to the terms or opened the account. Federal consumer protection laws do not permit a company to presume consent simply because a template agreement exists. 

4. Payment History Does Not Establish XXXX XXXX also relies on payment history and account activity as evidence that the account is valid. Payment activity, however, does not prove that I opened or authorized the account. Fraudulent accounts are often used, funded, and even partially paid by third parties for various reasons, including testing stolen credentials or maintaining the appearance of legitimacy. 

The presence of payments does not negate identity theft and does not establish consumer authorization. Treating payment history as proof of ownership is inconsistent with FCRA standards. 

5. FTC Identity Theft Report Was Improperly Discounted I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report affirming under penalty of perjury that I do not own this account. This report is a legally recognized document created specifically to protect consumers from being held responsible for fraudulent accounts. 

XXXX response effectively discounts the FTC Identity Theft Report by asserting that its internal findings override my sworn statement. This approach is inconsistent with the purpose and legal weight of an FTC Identity Theft Report and undermines the protections XXXX intended for identity theft victims. 

Once identity theft is asserted and supported by an FTC report, the burden shifts to the furnisher to demonstrate ownership with competent evidence. XXXX has not met this burden. 

6. Failure to Produce Documentary Proof of Ownership At no point has XXXX produced documentary proof that I personally opened or authorized this account. Specifically, XXXX has not provided : A signed application or contract Authenticated electronic signature records IP address logs associated with account creation Device fingerprinting or geolocation data tied to me Third-party identity verification documentation Without this evidence, the account can not be reasonably verified as belonging to me. XXXX requires proof, not assumptions based on system checks. 

7. Continued Reporting Causes Ongoing Harm The continued reporting of this account as charged off or delinquent causes ongoing harm to my credit profile, financial reputation, and access to credit. Identity theft victims should not be required to endure prolonged damage while furnishers rely on internal conclusions rather than producing proof. 

The FCRA exists to ensure maximum possible accuracy in consumer reporting. Allowing unverifiable accounts to remain reported defeats this purpose. 

8. Closure of Prior CFPB Case Does Not Resolve the Dispute My prior CFPB case # XXXX was closed, but that closure did not resolve the underlying issue. XXXX did not provide the requested proof, did not address the substance of my identity theft claim, and did not correct the reporting. 

This new case exists because the dispute remains unresolved. The closure of a prior case does not validate inaccurate reporting or relieve XXXX of its ongoing obligations under federal law. 

9. What a Reasonable Investigation Should Have Included A reasonable investigation in this matter should have included : A review of whether a signed or authenticated agreement exists Examination of account-opening IP addresses and devices Assessment of whether identity verification exceeded self-reported data Consideration of the FTC Identity Theft Report as substantive evidence Evaluation of whether ownership can be proven, not merely asserted Absent these steps, the investigation is incomplete. 

10. Required Corrective Actions To resolve this matter fairly and in compliance with the FCRA, XXXX must take XXXX of the following actions : Provide competent documentary proof that I personally opened and authorized the account, including signed or authenticated consent and identity verification evidence, or Delete the Kikoff tradeline from all consumer reporting agencies due to inability to verify ownership following an identity theft claim. 

Anything short of these actions leaves inaccurate and unverifiable information on my credit file. 

11. Request for Written Confirmation As part of a fair resolution, I also request written confirmation that : I am not responsible for the disputed account No further reporting or verification will occur The account will not be sold, assigned, or transferred The tradeline will not reappear in the future This confirmation is necessary to prevent continued or future harm. 

12. Why This Resolution Is Fair The resolution requested is fair because : I acted promptly and in good faith I followed all required procedures to report identity theft I provided sworn documentation XXXX failed to meet its burden of proof I am not requesting monetary compensation or special treatment. I am requesting accuracy, verification, and compliance with federal consumer protection laws. 

13. Closing XXXX XXXX conclusion, I am creating this new CFPB case because my prior case # XXXX was closed without resolving the dispute. I do not agree with XXXX XXXX conclusions. I do not own this account. I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report because the account is fraudulent. 

A fair resolution requires Kikoff Lending , LLC to either produce competent proof of account ownership or delete the account from my credit reports. Continued reporting without proof violates the spirit and letter of the Fair Credit Reporting Act and perpetuates harm to an identity theft victim. 

I respectfully request continued CFPB oversight to ensure this matter is resolved lawfully and fairly. 

Thank you for your time and attention.

On XX/XX/XXXX, I deposited {$23000.00} in cash into my personal account at Truist Bank. The bank accepted the deposit at the branch, credited the transaction, and issued a deposit receipt, confirming that the funds were received by Truist. This transaction was completed in person and involved cash only, not a check, wire transfer, ACH, or electronic instrument. 

Shortly after the deposit, Truist Bank placed the funds on administrative hold, claiming the deposit was suspected of fraud. I was never provided with any written notice, fraud determination, supporting documentation, or legal explanation justifying this hold. No law enforcement agency contacted me, and I was never informed of any court order, seizure notice, or governmental action involving these funds. 

On XX/XX/XXXX, Truist Bank closed my account while still retaining the {$23000.00}. Despite closing the account, Truist did not issue a cashiers check, refund, or remittance of the remaining balance. I also did not receive any written explanation regarding the continued retention of my money after account closure. 

From XX/XX/XXXX onward, Truist Bank provided no updates, no correspondence, and no resolution regarding my funds. I did not receive periodic notices, status letters, or requests for additional information. For over XXXX year, Truist remained silent while continuing to hold my money. 

When I contacted Truist again after this prolonged period, I was told that the funds were still on hold and that Truist had allegedly contacted another institution that supposedly confirmed the deposit was fraud. This explanation is false, misleading, and illogical, as the transaction in question was a cash deposit, not a negotiable instrument or inter-bank transaction. There is no external institution that can verify or invalidate a cash deposit once accepted by a bank. 

To this day, Truist Bank continues to retain my {$23000.00} without returning it, without providing legally required documentation, and without citing any valid statutory or court-ordered authority. 

IMPROPER CLASSIFICATION OF A CASH DEPOSIT AS FRAUD Truist Banks assertion that a cash deposit was determined to be fraudulent is fundamentally flawed. Cash, by its nature, is not drawn on another institution, does not rely on third-party authorization, and is not subject to return once accepted unless it is proven counterfeit or seized pursuant to lawful authority. 

At no point did Truist : Claim the cash was counterfeit Provide a Secret Service or law enforcement notice Provide a seizure receipt or forfeiture documentation Provide a court order authorizing retention Once Truist accepted the cash deposit and issued a receipt, the funds became a bank liability owed to the depositor, not contingent property subject to indefinite internal review. 

VIOLATIONS OF UCC ARTICLE 4 ( BANK DEPOSITS AND COLLECTIONS ) Under Uniform Commercial Code Article 4, when a bank accepts funds for deposit, it assumes responsibility for proper handling and settlement. Although Article 4 commonly addresses items such as checks, its principles regarding finality of acceptance, accountability, and timely disposition apply here. 

By accepting the cash and crediting the account, Truist completed the transaction. There is no UCC provision permitting a bank to hold deposited funds indefinitely without : Written notice A lawful basis A defined resolution process Truists actions constitute wrongful retention and conversion of funds, as the bank continues to exercise control over money that legally belongs to the depositor. 

VIOLATIONS OF CONSUMER FINANCIAL PROTECTION PRINCIPLES Federal consumer protection law requires banks to act in a manner that is : Transparent Fair Timely Supported by documentation Truist violated these principles by : Failing to provide written notice of the hold Closing the account without returning remaining funds Failing to communicate for over XXXX year Providing contradictory and unsupported explanations Under CFPB unfair, deceptive, or abusive acts or practices ( UDAAP ) standards, it is unfair and abusive for a financial institution to : Retain consumer funds indefinitely Withhold legally required explanations Shift the burden onto the consumer without due process DUE PROCESS AND UNLAWFUL CONVERSION OF FUNDS Truist Banks conduct also violates basic due process principles. If a bank believes funds are connected to unlawful activity, the proper course is to : Notify law enforcement Freeze funds pursuant to a legal hold Provide notice to the customer None of these steps occurred. 

There is no legal authority allowing a private bank to permanently retain customer funds based solely on an internal suspicion, particularly when : No crime has been charged No forfeiture proceeding exists No court order has been issued By continuing to hold my {$23000.00} without lawful authority, Truist is engaging in conversion, defined as the unauthorized assumption and exercise of ownership over property belonging to another. 

ACCOUNT CLOSURE WITHOUT REMITTANCE When Truist closed my account on XX/XX/XXXX, it had a duty to : Return the remaining balance Issue a cashiers check Or provide instructions for remittance Truist did none of these. Closing an account does not extinguish the banks obligation to return customer funds. Retaining the balance after closure, without legal authority, is improper and unlawful. 

FAILURE TO PROVIDE REQUIRED DISCLOSURES AND NOTICES At no time did Truist provide : A fraud determination letter A hold notice explaining duration and legal basis A seizure or forfeiture notice A right-to-appeal or dispute process This lack of disclosure violates basic banking standards and deprives the consumer of the ability to challenge the banks actions. 

ONGOING HARM AND FINANCIAL INJURY As a result of Truist Banks actions, I have suffered : Loss of access to {$23000.00} of my own money Prolonged financial uncertainty Emotional distress Significant time and effort attempting to resolve the issue The harm is ongoing, as the funds remain unlawfully withheld. 

REQUESTED RESOLUTION I am requesting that Truist Bank be required to do XXXX of the following immediately : Release and return the full {$23000.00} without further delay, OR Provide a written explanation, including : The exact legal authority relied upon Any court order or law enforcement directive The date and basis of any alleged fraud determination Absent such documentation, Truist has no lawful right to continue holding my funds. 

CONCLUSION Truist Bank accepted my cash deposit on XX/XX/XXXX, closed my account on XX/XX/XXXX, and has retained my money for over a year without lawful justification. This conduct violates consumer protection principles, UCC banking obligations, and fundamental fairness. 

I respectfully request the CFPBs assistance in compelling Truist Bank to resolve this matter promptly and return my funds.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I am writing to formally complain about Krakens failure to provide me with any advance notice regarding the delisting of crypto currency XXXX  As a result of this lack of notification, I was unable to trade the asset in a timely manner under reasonable conditions. The coin is no longer listed on any other major exchange, forcing me to consider swapping it at current severely depressed liquidity levels, which would result in an approximate 80 % loss of my holdings value. 

Krakens own policies and announcements typically include advance notice for scheduled delistings ( often via email, platform notifications, blog posts, or support articles ), allowing users sufficient time to act. In cases where advance notice is possible, Kraken has stated it will notify clients accordingly. The complete absence of any such communication in my casedespite my account being active and notifications enabledconstitutes a failure to meet reasonable expectations of fair treatment and transparency. 

This lack of notice has directly caused me significant financial harm. Under Californias Digital Financial Assets Law ( DFAL ) ( effective XX/XX/year>, with ongoing consumer protection obligations ), licensed digital financial asset businesses like Kraken are required to implement policies and procedures for ceasing to list or offer digital assets, including notification to affected consumers. While the DFAL emphasizes broader consumer protections, risk disclosures, and fair practices, the failure to notify users ahead of a delisting that materially impacts their holdings may violate these principles and general California consumer protection standards against unfair or deceptive acts. 

Additionally, federal consumer protection laws enforced by bodies such as the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau ( CFPB ) address issues in crypto-asset services, including transparency in platform operations and handling of user assets. A pattern of inadequate notifications could raise concerns under these frameworks. Krakens terms of service also generally reserve the right to delist but often imply reasonable user protections in practice, and sudden unnotified actions without extenuating circumstances ( which do not appear to apply here ) undermine user trust and may breach implied duties of good faith. 

Below is there response admitting they failed to properly send notification. 

" A notification regarding the planned delisting was prepared and scheduled for distribution on XX/XX/year> to affected clients in the United States and XXXX. Although the notice was generated with the intent of alerting you in advance, it unfortunately did not reach your inbox despite your notification settings being enabled. We sincerely regret that this communication did not reach you and understand how receiving that notification in time could have affected your ability to manage your holdings differently. ''

Capital One escalations became involved and the matter was treated as a formal complaint. 

Throughout this process, Capital One provided inconsistent and misleading guidance. We requested an unwind/cancellation of the funded loan due to material misrepresentation and were told multiple times that Capital One could not unwind a fully funded auto loan. This is inconsistent with our prior experience with Capital One unwinding a funded auto loan in the past, and inconsistent with later actions Capital One participated in. 

Capital Ones Executive Response Team ( Presidents Office ) later advised that the dealership could cancel the original contract and submit a corrected contract. We were physically present at the dealership with the General Manager while the dealership called Capital One, reversed the original contract funding by phone, and submitted the corrected contract. Capital Ones actions have created a risk of inaccurate furnishing of information to credit bureaus in violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ). Midlands response confirms that the accounts have been marked Cease and Desist and that they will no longer contact me. However, this action alone does not constitute a fair or complete resolution, as the disputed tradelines continue to appear on my consumer credit reports, causing ongoing harm. 

Key Issues With the Companys Response Accounts Do Not Belong to Me ( Identity Theft ) These accounts were opened fraudulently and do not belong to me. I filed an FTC Identity Theft report and formally disputed ownership. Once identity theft is asserted, continued reporting without conclusive proof of ownership is improper under the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ).

Failure to Delete Fraudulent Tradelines Midland admits it does not possess : An original signed contract bearing my signature A complete, original payment history from account origination Proof that I personally applied for or authorized these accounts Instead, they rely solely on seller-provided data. While Midland states such documentation is not required under the FDCPA, credit reporting accuracy is governed by the FCRA, not the FDCPA. Under FCRA 623 ( b ), information that can not be fully verified must be deleted, especially when identity theft is claimed.

Improper and Misleading Credit Reporting Midland acknowledges that the open date reported is the date of purchase, not the original account opening date. This practice misrepresents account history and unfairly harms my credit profile. 

Cease and Desist Does Not Resolve Fraud Marking an account Cease and Desist only stops communications. It does not : Establish ownership Cure fraudulent reporting Satisfy identity theft protections Continuing to report accounts while ceasing collection activity is inconsistent and unreasonable. 

No Confirmation of Deletion Requests to Credit Bureaus Midland does not confirm that it submitted a formal request to delete the tradelines with : XXXX XXXX XXXX  Without this confirmation, the relief described is incomplete.

The billing statements and summaries Midland attached do not prove that I incurred or authorized these debts and do not override my identity theft claim XXXX, XXXX.

Consumer complaint narrative:
I respectfully disagree with the companys response and conclusions. I do not own the accounts referenced ( Account Numbers XXXX and XXXX ), and I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report stating that these accounts are fraudulent. I am submitting this feedback and creating a new CFPB case because the previous case was closed without resolving the identity-theft issue under the controlling provisions of the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ). 

The companys response relies almost entirely on FDCPA verification standards and internal review. However, FDCPA XXXX does not establish ownership and does not override identity-theft protections under FCRA XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX confirm that a debt exists in a creditors records, but it does not prove that I opened, authorized, or benefited from the account. Once an FTC Identity Theft Report is filed, credit reporting agencies are required to block identity-theft-related information, and furnishers must reassess whether continued furnishing is lawful. 

The company acknowledges it is a data furnisher and does not own the accounts. As a furnisher, it still has obligations under FCRA 623 ( a ) to ensure accuracy and to stop furnishing information it knows or should know is inaccurate once identity theft has been asserted. Repeating information supplied by a clientwithout original proof of my authorizationdoes not satisfy this obligation. 

The response also requests that I provide proof that I did not set up services at a specific address or provide a police report. The FCRA does not require a police report to trigger identity-theft blocking when an FTC Identity Theft Report has been submitted. The burden is not on the consumer to disprove a debt after identity theft is asserted ; rather, the law requires blocking unless the report is shown to be materially false. 

Importantly, the companys response does not provide : A signed application or contract bearing my signature ; Proof of identity verification at account origination ; Evidence that I personally authorized or benefited from the accounts ; or Evidence rebutting my FTC Identity Theft Report. 

Because these deficiencies remain, the accounts should be blocked and removed, and reinsertion protections must be enforced. Closing the prior CFPB case did not resolve the issue, which is why I am pursuing this matter through a new case and requesting CFPB oversight to ensure compliance with FCRA 605B and 611 ( a ) ( XXXX ) ( B ). 

I respectfully request that the CFPB note that : I do not own these accounts ; I filed an FTC Identity Theft Report ; FDCPA verification does not resolve identity theft ; FCRA requires blocking and suppression of fraudulent information ; and Continued treatment of these accounts as valid causes ongoing harm.

LVNV Funding has engaged in a pattern of systemic noncompliance by : Ignoring statutory cease-collection requirements Substituting boilerplate documentation for lawful validation Continuing to damage my consumer report without legal authority This conduct undermines the integrity of the consumer reporting system and warrants regulatory intervention.

I am filing a complaint regarding improper handling of Private Mortgage Insurance ( PMI ) under the Homeowners Protection Act.

My mortgage loan was formally recast ( re-amortized ) in XX/XX/2025, following a lender-approved principal curtailment. As part of this recast, the amortization schedule was revised. My LTV dropped to well below 78 %.

Under 12 U.S.C. 4901 ( 18 ), scheduled amortization includes an amortization schedule as modified by the lender and the borrower.

Under 12 U.S.C. 4902 ( b ), PMI must terminate automatically when the principal balance, based on the scheduled amortization ( or as otherwise modified ), is first scheduled to reach 78 % of the original value of the property.

Despite the recast in XX/XX/2025 and the existence of a modified amortization schedule, the current loan servicer failed to update the PMI termination date and collected PMI for months before transferring my loan, effectively disregarding the lender-approved re-amortization.

I have requested confirmation of the PMI termination date using the post-recast amortization schedule, but the servicer has failed to provide a legally supported explanation for continuing to rely on the original schedule.

I am requesting : 1. Written confirmation that PMI termination is being calculated using the post-recast amortization schedule, consistent with 12 U.S.C. 4901 ( 18 ) and 4902 ( b ) ; or 2. A written legal justification, citing specific statutory or regulatory authority, explaining why a lender-approved recast does not qualify as a modified amortization schedule under the Homeowners Protection Act.

3. That all PMI payments collected after the mortgage recast and LTV below 78 % date are refunded to me.

I am filing this complaint against Exeter Finance LLC for failure to provide a required credit application decision notice in violation of the Equal Credit Opportunity Act ( ECOA ), 15 U.S.C. 1691 ( d ), and its implementing regulation, Regulation B, 12 CFR 1002.9. The facts supporting this complaint are as follows : XXXX or about XX/XX/XXXX, I visited XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX Nevada, XXXX purchase a XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ). As part of the vehicle purchase process, the dealership submitted my credit application to Exeter Finance LLC for financing consideration. 2.Exeter Finance LLC accessed my consumer credit report on XX/XX/XXXX, which is confirmed by a hard inquiry visible on my credit report from that date. This hard inquiry is direct evidence that Exeter Finance received my credit application, deemed it complete enough to warrant a credit pull, and began evaluating it. Under the Fair Credit Reporting Act, accessing a consumer 's credit report requires a permissible purpose, and in this case that purpose was my credit application. 3.Despite pulling my credit report and evaluating my application, Exeter Finance LLC has never provided me with any notice of the decision on my application. I have received no approval notice, no adverse action notice, no denial letter, and no counteroffer. Under ECOA and Regulation B, a creditor is required to notify the applicant in writing of the action taken on a completed credit application within 30 days. As of the date of this complaint more than 60 days after the application date I have received no such notice. 4.When I contacted Exeter Finance directly to request a copy of the decision on my application, I was told to ask the dealership. This response is wholly inadequate and does not satisfy Exeter 's statutory obligation. Under ECOA, the duty to notify the applicant of the credit decision rests with the creditor in this case, Exeter Finance not with the dealership that served as an intermediary. The dealership can not fulfill the creditor 's obligation under federal law, and Exeter 's attempt to redirect me to a third party is itself a violation of the Act. 5.The vehicle was ultimately financed through XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX annual percentage rate of 17.87 % over a term of 68 months. Without knowing whether Exeter Finance approved my application and, if so, at what rate and terms I can not determine whether I was placed into less favorable financing when better terms may have been available. This lack of transparency raises serious concerns about potential dealer rate markup and financing steering practices, which are exactly the kinds of harms that ECOA 's disclosure requirements are intended to prevent. 6.I have sent a formal written demand to Exeter Finance LLC via XXXX XXXX Mail XXXX XXXX Receipt Requested, dated XX/XX/XXXX, demanding that they provide the decision notice within 30 days. I am filing this CFPB complaint concurrently to create an official record of Exeter 's non-compliance and to seek the Bureau 's assistance in compelling Exeter to fulfill its legal obligations.

Paypal Case ID : XXXX Paypal Transaction ID : XXXX I am a long-term PayPal business seller. I have been selling with PayPal since 2013 and have relied on PayPal as the primary payment processor for my luxury resale Shopify store. As a long-term business user, I relied on PayPals representations regarding Seller Protection and fraud protection when accepting payments.

PayPal advertises XXXX XXXX and fraud protection for merchants and flagged this transaction as low chargeback risk at the time of sale. 

Despite this, PayPal removed {$1300.00} from my business account and charged a dispute fee after a buyer filed a bank chargeback months after delivery. The funds were debited automatically with the dispute reason listed only as Other, without any clear explanation, policy citation, or meaningful review of the evidence I submitted.

I provided documentation showing the item was accurately described, delivered successfully, and shipped as listed. However, PayPal did not clearly disclose why XXXX XXXX was denied, did not identify what specific policy exclusion applied, and did not provide a transparent or fair appeal process. 

As a result of PayPals actions, my business account was left with a negative balance and my ability to use PayPal services was restricted. As a small business, my financials were directly and materially impacted. The loss of funds disrupted cash flow, affected my ability to operate day-to-day, and limited my ability to accept payments. This financial harm occurred without clear disclosure, transparent justification, or a meaningful opportunity to appeal PayPals decision.

I believe PayPals seller protection and dispute handling practices are confusing, misleading, and inconsistent with how these protections are marketed to small business sellers.

PayPals current dispute and seller protection practices appear to favor buyer claims by default, even when sellers provide clear documentation and evidence. This creates an environment where chargeback abuse and bad-faith buyer behavior are not meaningfully addressed, leaving honest sellers financially exposed and without adequate protection. 
While I understand that PayPal does not have authority over final decisions made by card-issuing financial institutions in chargebacks, PayPal continues to market Seller Protection and fraud protection to merchants without clearly disclosing the limited nature of these protections in bank-initiated disputes. In practice, sellers bear the financial loss even when documentation is provided, which creates an imbalance that leaves small businesses exposed to chargeback abuse and bad-faith buyer claims.

PayPal charges sellers significant transaction fees, often totaling approximately 4 % per transaction, while marketing XXXX XXXX as a benefit of using its platform. Historically, PayPal maintained mechanisms to absorb or offset certain losses related to disputes. Today, however, sellers are required to bear the full financial impact of bank chargebacks, even when PayPal collects fees, controls the transaction flow, and benefits from seller reliance on its platform. This imbalance raises concerns about whether PayPals XXXX XXXX program provides meaningful protection relative to the fees charged to small business sellers.

I am filing this complaint against LVNV Funding LLC, a known junk debt buyer, for unlawfully reporting an alleged collection account that I had no prior knowledge of and for failing to comply with federal debt collection and credit reporting laws. I never received any written notice, dunning letter, notice of rights, or initial communication regarding this alleged debt before it was placed on my credit report. I do not recognize this account. I do not know what this alleged debt is for, who the original creditor is, or how LVNV claims to have acquired it. The absence of written notice is a direct violation of FDCPA 1692g ( a ), which requires a debt collector to provide written notice of the debt within five days of initial communication. Despite never providing written notice, LVNV has engaged in aggressive collection activity, including an excessive number of phone calls. Repeated calls without providing written validation constitute harassment and unfair collection practices under FDCPA 1692d and 1692f. I have filed complaints regarding this matter with the FTC and my state Attorney Generals office due to the seriousness of these violations. LVNV Funding has a well-documented history of consumer lawsuits, regulatory actions, and allegations involving the collection and reporting of unverified debts. Their conduct in this matter reflects a continued pattern of reckless disregard for consumer rights. Upon discovering this account on my credit report, I requested proper validation. To date, LVNV has provided no lawful validation. I am fully aware that validation requires far more than internal account notes, a balance statement, or a generic data sheet. Proper and lawful validation of an alleged debt includes all of the following : The original signed contract, application, or agreement bearing my signature. Complete billing and payment history from the original creditor. An itemized accounting of the alleged balance, including principal, interest, fees, penalties, and charges. Documentation showing the date of default. Documentation showing the date of charge-off, if applicable. Proof that the amount demanded matches the original creditors records. A complete chain of title demonstrating every sale, assignment, or transfer of the debt from the original creditor to LVNV Funding. Proof that LVNV legally owns the debt and has the authority to collect. Documentation showing the alleged debt is within the applicable statute of limitations. Proof that the information furnished to the credit bureaus is complete, accurate, and verifiable. None of this documentation has been provided. Despite the lack of validation, LVNV continues to furnish this account to the credit bureaus as accurate. Furnishing a disputed and unverified debt violates FCRA 1681s-2 ( b ), which requires a reasonable investigation upon notice of dispute, and FCRA 1681e ( b ), which requires reasonable procedures to ensure maximum possible accuracy. XXXX XXXX reporting standards require data to be complete, consistent, and supported by documentationstandards that have not been met here. I am calling on the CFPB to hold LVNV Funding accountable for these violations. Using the credit reporting system as leverage to collect an unverified debt while failing to provide notice or validation is unlawful.

I am filing this complaint against Equifax for unlawfully reporting two collection accounts on my credit file with no identifiable furnisher. 
The two accounts are : XXXX XXXX {$0.00} XXXX XXXX {$220.00} On my Equifax credit report, the furnisher name is listed as the same numeric string as the account number. No company name, address, or identifying creditor is provided. This means Equifax is publishing anonymous collection accounts. 
This is a direct violation of federal law. 
Under FCRA 609 ( a ) ( 1 ) and 602, I have the right to know the identity of any party furnishing information about me. Equifax can not legally report derogatory accounts from unidentified entities. 
Under FCRA 607 ( b ), Equifax must maintain maximum possible accuracy. Reporting a collection account without a company name is inherently inaccurate and unverifiable.

Under FCRA 611 ( a ), Equifax is required to conduct a reasonable reinvestigation. A reinvestigation is impossible when no furnisher identity exists.

Under FCRA 623 ( a ) ( 1 ) ( A ), a furnisher can not furnish information without identifying itself.

Under FDCPA 807 ( 2 ) ( A ), an anonymous collection account is misleading.

Under FDCPA 809 ( b ), I am denied my right to validation because no collector is identified.

Under Metro-2 reporting standards, a collection tradeline must include a valid creditor name, identification, and contact information. These entries fail Metro-2 compliance. 
I disputed these accounts more than 90 days ago. Equifax stated it needed additional time. The statutory investigation period has long expired. Federal law does not allow indefinite extensions.

Because the furnisher can not be identified, these accounts are legally unverifiable. When information can not be verified, FCRA requires deletion.

Equifax has now willfully continued reporting two anonymous collection accounts despite knowing : No furnisher identity exists No validation is possible No lawful investigation can occur The statutory reinvestigation clock has expired This constitutes willful noncompliance under FCRA 616 and negligent noncompliance under 617. 
I am demanding immediate deletion of both collection accounts from my Equifax credit file. 
If Equifax can not identify the furnisher, provide validation, and demonstrate lawful Metro-2 compliance, these accounts must be permanently removed.

I am submitting this complaint regarding a collection account reported by IQ Data XXXX XXXX XXXX in the amount of {$2500.00}, which currently appears on my consumer credit reports. 

On XX/XX/year>XXXX I sent a debt validation request to IQ Data XXXX XXXX XXXX via certified mail to their official mailing address. This request was made pursuant to the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act ( FDCPA ), 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( b ). In this letter, I formally disputed the debt and requested full validation, including but not limited to documentation bearing my physical signature and evidence establishing that the alleged debt belongs to me and my partner. 

According to USPS tracking records, the certified letter was successfully delivered and picked up by IQ Data XXXX XXXX XXXX. Despite receipt of my validation request, IQ Data XXXX has failed to provide any of the requested documentation or otherwise respond. Under the FDCPA, once a consumer disputes a debt in writing, the debt collector must cease all collection activity until proper verification of the debt is provided. Continuing to report or verify the debt to consumer reporting agencies without first validating it constitutes continued collection activity and is a violation of 15 U.S.C. 1692g ( b ). 

Additionally, I disputed this collection account with all three major consumer reporting agencies ( XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX pursuant to the Fair Credit Reporting Act ( FCRA ), 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 and 1681i. I explained that the debt had not been validated and that the collector failed to respond to my certified validation request. Despite this, the credit bureaus reported the account as verified. 

When I requested clarification from the credit bureaus regarding how the debt was verified as accurate, I did not receive a meaningful explanation or documentation describing the method of verification. Under the FCRA, consumer reporting agencies are required to conduct a reasonable investigation and to provide consumers, upon request, a description of the procedure used to determine the accuracy and completeness of the information, as required by 15 U.S.C. 1681i ( a ) ( 6 ) ( B ) ( iii ).

Furthermore, furnishing or verifying information that has not been substantiated after a dispute may constitute a violation of 15 U.S.C. 1681s-2 ( b ), which requires furnishers of information to investigate disputes and report only accurate and verifiable information. 

At this time, the collection account remains on my credit reports despite : A timely written dispute and validation request sent to the debt collector ; Verified receipt of that request by the collector ; No validation or documentation provided by the collector ; No clear or reasonable explanation from the credit bureaus regarding how the debt was verified. 

I am requesting the CFPBs assistance in investigating this matter and ensuring compliance with the FDCPA and FCRA, including requiring IQ Data XXXX XXXX XXXX and the consumer reporting agencies to either provide proper validation and verification or remove the collection account from my credit reports. 

Thank you for your time and attention to this matter.

I paid a merchant for home improvement services in the District of Columbia. After payment was made, I discovered the merchant was not licensed as required under applicable District of Columbia home improvement regulations, and thus did not have legal authority to accept payment for the services provided. The work was also not code-complaint, and I had to redo a lot of the work.

Under District of Columbia Municipal Regulations, no person shall require or accept any payment for a home improvement contract unless properly licensed as a home improvement contractor or as a licensed salesperson employed by a licensed contractor. 16 DCMR 800.1. The regulations define home improvement work broadly to include remodeling, repair, alteration, improvement, or replacement of residential property. Any money paid to an unlicensed contractor is recoverable by the homeowner. 


I provided American Express with documentation showing : The charges were for home improvement services performed in the XXXX XXXX XXXX 

The merchant was not licensed as required by XXXX XXXX XXXX law. 

Under 16 DCMR 800.1, the merchant had no legal authority to accept payment and the contract is therefore void and any payments are recoverable. 


Despite receiving this information, American Express denied my dispute and allowed the merchant to retain payment from an unlawful transaction, stating that the merchant claimed that there were no issues with quality of the work ( false- the work was not code compliant ) and that I never asked if the merchant is licensed ( irrelevant ). 


By refusing to reverse charges arising from a transaction that was unlawful under District of Columbia law, American Express facilitated and upheld an illegal transaction in violation of the Fair Credit Billing Act and failed to protect my rights as a consumer. American Express did not provide any legal justification grounded in statute or regulation for allowing an unlicensed merchant to retain funds obtained through an unlawful transaction. 


This is not a simple service-quality dispute. The underlying transaction was unlawful because the merchant lacked the license required under District of Columbia law, and American Express was put on notice of the illegality yet still refused to correct the billing error. 


Please see attached the dispute letter. I would be happy to provide any other evidence as requested.

Product: Credit reporting or other personal consumer reports
Consumer complaint narrative: I am submitting this complaint regarding an XXXX account that appears on my credit report as a derogatory account and does not belong to me. This account was not opened, authorized, or agreed to by me and is the result of identity theft. Despite my efforts to address this issue through proper channels, the account continues to be reported inaccurately. I first became aware of this XXXX account after reviewing my credit reports and noticing a negative tradeline associated with Affirm that I did not recognize. I have never applied for credit with XXXX for this account, never agreed to any loan or installment terms, and never received or benefited from any goods, services, or funds connected to it. I immediately recognized that this account was fraudulent and opened without my knowledge or consent. Upon discovering the account, I took prompt and responsible action. I filed an Identity Theft Report with the Federal Trade Commission ( FTC ), declaring under penalty of perjury that this Affirm account was opened fraudulently and does not belong to me. This report was submitted in good faith and accurately reflects that I am a victim of identity theft. After filing the FTC identity theft report, I disputed the XXXX account and requested validation. In my disputes, I clearly stated that I do not own this account and that it was opened through identity theft. I requested that XXXX provide documentation proving that I am legally responsible for the alleged debt. Specifically, I requested evidence such as : A signed or electronically executed loan agreement or contract Proof of my authorization or consent to open the account Identity verification records used at the time of account origination Account statements or transaction history Proof that goods, services, or funds were delivered to or received by me Despite these requests, Affirm has not provided competent, original documentation establishing that I am responsible for this account. No signed agreement, no proof of authorization, and no evidence of identity verification tying me to this account have been produced. Without such documentation, there is no factual or legal basis to continue associating this account with my credit profile. In some responses, the account has been described as verified or left reported while marked as disputed. However, simply relying on internal records or automated confirmation does not constitute proper verification in an identity theft case. Verification must be based on actual evidence showing that the consumer opened and agreed to the account. That evidence has not been provided. The continued reporting of this XXXX account is inaccurate and misleading. It falsely represents my credit history and financial behavior and causes ongoing harm. Negative credit reporting can affect access to credit, interest rates, employment opportunities, housing decisions, and overall financial stability. As a victim of identity theft, I should not be required to repeatedly dispute the same fraudulent account or bear the burden of proving a negative when the reporting company can not substantiate its claim. I want to be clear that this is not a billing dispute and not a disagreement over loan terms, balances, or payments. I am not refusing to pay a legitimate debt. I am asserting that no legitimate debt exists between me and Affirm because I did not open or authorize this account. There is no valid contractual relationship. I have acted responsibly and in good faith throughout this process. I reviewed my credit reports, identified the fraudulent account, filed an FTC identity theft report, disputed the account, and requested validation. The failure to correct the reporting despite these steps has left me with no choice but to escalate this matter through the CFPB. An account that was opened through identity theft and can not be validated should not remain on a consumers credit report in any status. Marking the account as disputed or leaving it reported during an investigation does not remedy the harm caused by fraudulent reporting. I am submitting this complaint so that the XXXX account can be properly investigated and removed in full. Fraudulent accounts should be blocked, deleted, and permanently removed once identity theft has been documented and the account can not be substantiated. I respectfully request that this matter be reviewed thoroughly and that XXXX be required to correct the inaccurate reporting so that my credit reports accurately reflect my true credit history and do not include an account that was opened through identity theft.

Issue: Advertising and marketing, including promotional offers
Consumer complaint narrative:
I am filing this complaint regarding misleading promotional disclosures and undisclosed conditions tied to a Citi credit card balance transfer offer. 

I previously filed a CFPB complaint related to improper payment allocation. That complaint was closed after Citi responded. However, Citis written response introduced a previously undisclosed condition that materially alters how the promotional XXXX operates. This complaint addresses that disclosure issue. 

Citi promoted a balance transfer as 0 % XXXX until XX/XX/year>, after which the XXXX increased to approximately 20.24 % ( annual XXXX ). Based on this disclosure, a reasonable consumer would believe that making payment by the promotional end dateor immediately afterwould avoid interest at the higher rate. 

In Citis written response to CFPB and to the XXXX XXXX Attorney General, Citi stated : In order for the payment to be applied to the expiring balance transfer, the account must cycle before the promotional interest rate is updated to the purchase rate. 

This account cycle requirement was never disclosed in the promotional offer, cardmember agreement, or any balance transfer terms provided to me. 

More importantly, Citis explanation creates a practical impossibility for the consumer to avoid interest : 1. If I made a payment before XX/XX/year>, Citis own payment allocation rules would require that payment to be applied to a different promotional balance with a lower APR ( 0.99 % ), not to the expiring balance transfer. This would not protect me from post-expiration interest. 
2. If I made the payment on or after XX/XX/year>, the date the XXXX increased, Citi claims the payment could not be properly applied unless the account had already cycledan undisclosed internal processing requirement. 

As a result, there was no disclosed or reasonable way for me to comply with the promotion as advertised and avoid interest. The promotional statement of 0 % APR until XX/XX/year> is therefore misleading, because interest liability is actually determined by an undisclosed statement cycle, not the advertised date. 

An undisclosed timing condition that determines whether interest is charged is a material term and must be clearly disclosed. Citis reliance on internal processing rules to deny the consumer the benefit of the advertised promotional APR constitutes misrepresentation by omission. 

Because this logic would apply to any consumer with multiple promotional balances, this appears to be a systemic disclosure issue affecting Citis balance transfer promotions. 

I respectfully request CFPB review of whether Citis promotional disclosures and practices comply with federal consumer protection and Truth in Lending requirements.

Specifically : 45 C.F.R. 164.502 ( a ) Prohibits the use or disclosure of protected health information except as permitted or required by HIPAA.

45 C.F.R. 164.508 ( a ) Requires valid written authorization from the patient for any disclosure not otherwise permitted.

45 C.F.R. 164.530 ( c ) Requires covered entities to safeguard medical information and prevent unauthorized disclosures.

This unauthorized disclosure has caused harm and violates my federally protected right to medical privacy. I am requesting immediate investigation, cessation of any further disclosures, and corrective action as required by law.

On XX/XX/year>, a XXXX XXXX check in the amount of {$1000.00} was issued by XXXX XXXX to the payee. The check was drawn on a XXXX XXXX account and sent through XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX service. 

On XX/XX/year>, the payee deposited the check into a Capital One account. Capital One received and imaged the check for processing ( the check image provided by XXXX XXXX shows a Capital One XXXX processing stamp, confirming presentment through Capital Ones clearing center ). 

After initial provisional posting, Capital One rejected the check at posting due to a payee name mismatch ( nickname vs. legal name ). Capital One states that the item was not accepted for final settlement and that a return was initiated. Capital One further states that it never received or retained final settlement funds for this item. 

However, XXXX XXXX system shows the check as cleared/paid, and XXXX XXXX states that no return was received. XXXX XXXX therefore has not recredited the drawers account and considers the item finally paid. 

As a result : The payee never received the funds. 
The drawer was never recredited.

The depositary bank states it rejected and returned the item and did not accept settlement. 
The paying bank states final payment occurred and no return exists. 

This creates a failed interbank return reconciliation / misapplied Federal Reserve settlement. Presentment is proven, posting was rejected, and the return did not reconcile. The funds are missing between institutions and are not in either customers account. 

This is an interbank settlement error governed by : Uniform Commercial Code ( UCC ) Articles 3 and 4 ( including 4-215 and 4-302 ) Regulation CC Federal Reserve Adjustment and Return Rules Under these rules, funds can not disappear, and one of the two institutions must either recredit the drawer or complete an interbank adjustment and credit the payee. 

The requested resolution is : A full Federal Reserve settlement and return trace by both institutions Identification of whether final settlement was accepted or whether a return failed to post Recredit or reissuance of the funds to the drawer pending interbank adjustment Written confirmation of the adjustment and final disposition of the funds. 

The consumer is requesting that the CFPB require both XXXX XXXX and Capital One to perform a formal interbank adjustment investigation, comply with UCC and Regulation CC obligations, and resolve the missing settlement so that the funds are restored to the rightful party.

While these limitations are disclosed in the fine print, they are not presented with comparable prominence to the headline marketing message. The marketing creates a strong impression of a broadly usable annual companion ticket, while the actual redemption process is highly constrained and difficult for many consumers to use successfully.

This creates a material gap between the perceived value used to justify the annual fee and the practical usability of the benefit.

This complaint alleges unfair, deceptive, and abusive acts or practices ( UDAAP ) by Nissan Motor Acceptance Company, LLC ( NMAC ) in connection with the servicing and collection of a consumer auto loan. Specifically, NMAC intentionally disabled payment access after a timely cure, manufactured a default, impaired consumer credit, authorized an unlawful repossession in breach of the peace, and coerced a lumpsum payoff under economic duress to recover the vehicle. 
NMACs conduct caused substantial consumer injury, was not reasonably avoidable, and provided no countervailing consumer benefit. The practices appear policydriven and capable of repetition, raising concerns beyond an isolated dispute. 

DETAILED STATEMENT OF FACTS Complainants entered into a retail installment contract serviced by NMAC for a XXXX  XXXX XXXX. The loan carried a 0 % interest rate, a material and valuable contractual benefit. 
Within a sixmonth period, two automatic payments were returned. With respect to the second returned payment, Complainants cured the issue before the contractual due date by making a manual payment that posted and cleared before the due date and exceeded the amount then due, placing the account in a paidahead status. 
Despite this timely

cure, NMAC intentionally disabled all online account access, including automatic payments, online payments, and access to account documents and notices. NMAC representatives confirmed this lockout resulted from an internal policy and refused reinstatement despite proof of cure. By disabling ordinary payment mechanisms, NMAC materially interfered with Complainants ability to make payments and foreseeably increased the risk of delinquency. Any alleged delinquency occurred only after NMAC created this
impediment. 
NMAC thereafter authorized a nonjudicial repossession without providing required notices of default, right to cure, or intent to repossess to either obligor.

The repossession was conducted at a residential property in breach of the peace, without announcement and without allowing retrieval of personal property. Highvalue personal items were missing upon recovery of the vehicle. 
The vehicle sustained damage during repossession, including tire and rim damage, followed by braking system malfunction. 
To recover their vehicle and mitigate further harm, Complainants were forced to pay the remaining loan balance under economic duress, without any meaningful alternative. 


UDAAP ANALYSIS UNFAIR PRACTICES Disabling payment access after cure, thereby creating delinquency risk Manufacturing default through servicer interference Authorizing repossession without required notices and in breach of the peace Coercing payment through wrongful deprivation of collateral These practices caused substantial consumer injury, were not reasonably avoidable, and provided no countervailing benefit. 

DECEPTIVE PRACTICES Failure to clearly disclose that payment access would remain disabled even after cure Omission of material information regarding the consequences of account lockouts Misleading servicing practices that obscured consumers ability to remain current ABUSIVE PRACTICES Taking unreasonable advantage of consumers inability to protect their interests once payment access was disabled Leveraging manufactured default and credit impairment to coerce payoff Exploiting servicing control to extract financial advantage CONSUMER HARM As a direct result of NMACs conduct, Complainants suffered : Loss of use of their vehicle Forced payoff under economic duress Property loss and vehicle damage Credit and reputational harm Significant emotional distress and financial strain

Company : Fair Collections & Outsourcing , Inc. ( FCO ) Issue type : Debt collection / Credit reporting Amount : Approximately {$270.00} I am submitting this complaint regarding Fair Collections & Outsourcing , Inc. ( FCO ) and its continued handling and reporting of a disputed debt. 
The alleged debt relates to approximately {$270.00} in utilities from a former apartment tenancy at XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, XXXX XXXX. I do not owe this debt. 
I vacated the apartment on XX/XX/year>. On XX/XX/year>, I paid my final months rent and all associated charges in full. The resident ledger reflects a {$0.00} balance as of XX/XX/year>. I completed a move-out walk-through and was cleared to vacate with no balance due.

Months after I moved out, and after a change in property management, charges were added to the ledger despite my lack of access to the unit or account. These charges were repeatedly reversed, written off, re-posted, and reversed again. The remaining balance appears to be the result of post-move-out accounting adjustments rather than unpaid charges.

Despite the dispute, FCO offered a settlement amount and stated that it would continue to report the account as accurate. FCO has not addressed the internal inconsistencies in the ledger or the documented {$0.00} balance at move-out.

FCOs response likewise appears to conflate credit reporting accuracy obligations under the Fair Credit Reporting Act with debt validation requirements under the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act. 
I am requesting that the CFPB review FCOs conduct, including continued reporting and collection posture on a debt that has been formally disputed without competent validation. I am seeking removal of any credit reporting related to this account and cessation of collection activity absent proper validation.
